summary: Specifies how X.509 version 3 public key certificates can be used for public key authentication in the Secure Shell protocol. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Lets a secure login use an official ID card signed by a trusted authority instead of a bare key.

questions: how does ssh verify a certificate chain
subtitle: How SSH servers and users can prove who they are with X.509 certificate chains instead of bare keys.

tldr.problem: SSH authentication with a bare public key only works if you already trust the link between that key and an identity, and many corporate and government environments manage identity with X.509 certificates instead.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines new SSH public key algorithms (x509v3-ssh-dss, x509v3-ssh-rsa, x509v3-rsa2048-sha256 and x509v3-ecdsa-sha2-*) whose key data is a chain of X.509v3 certificates plus optional OCSP responses.
tldr.outcome: SSH implementations can verify a peer's key through a chain to a trusted certificate authority. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 6187 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2011, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. It builds on RFC 5280 for certificate handling and on the SSH transport and authentication RFCs.

sections.title: Why Certificates in SSH
sections.content:
Two Secure Shell protocols use public key cryptography. The Transport Layer Protocol requires a digital signature algorithm (the public key algorithm) to authenticate the server to the client, and the User Authentication Protocol allows a signature to authenticate the client to the server (publickey authentication).

In both cases, security depends on how strongly the signing key is linked to the signer's identity. X.509 version 3 certificates provide that link with a chain of signatures from a trusted root certification authority and its intermediate authorities, and are used in many corporate and government environments for identity management.

The existing algorithms are ssh-dss, ssh-rsa, pgp-sign-dss, pgp-sign-rsa and ecdsa-sha2-*. PGP has its own way of binding keys to identities, so this document covers only the non-PGP ones. The new algorithms differ from them solely in using X.509v3 certificates to carry the signer's public key.
sections.plainLanguage: A bare key is like a name tag anyone could write. A certificate is a name tag that a trusted office has stamped, so people can believe it.

sections.title: The Four New Algorithms and Key Format
sections.content:
The RFC defines x509v3-ssh-dss, x509v3-ssh-rsa, x509v3-rsa2048-sha256 and the family x509v3-ecdsa-sha2-*. Keys from the ECDSA family can be used with the ecmqv-sha2 key exchange method.

For all of them, the key data is one or more X.509v3 certificates followed by zero or more OCSP responses. Putting OCSP responses in the data can save communication rounds and lets a client outside a private network receive them from a server behind a firewall. Each certificate and OCSP response MUST be DER-encoded ASN.1.

The constraints are:

  • The sender's certificate MUST come first and its key must match the algorithm in use; each following certificate MUST certify the one before it.
  • The self-signed root certificate MAY be omitted, but all intermediate certificates MUST be included.
  • Certificates and OCSP responses SHOULD be signed only with algorithms the peer lists in server_host_key_algorithms, though others MAY be used, and verifiers MUST be prepared to receive them.
  • OCSP responses can be in any order, and their number MUST NOT exceed the number of certificates.

On receipt, implementations MUST verify the chain according to Section 6.1 of RFC 5280 against a root of trust configured by the administrator or user. If no OCSP responses are provided, accepting the certificate is up to the implementation and administrator. If the certificate says its authority uses OCSP and no response is available, rejecting it is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: The package you send holds your stamped ID card, the cards of the offices that stamped it, and maybe a note saying the card has not been cancelled. The last stamp-office card can be left out because the other side already knows it.

sections.title: Certificate Extensions
sections.content:
Two X.509 extensions can restrict how a certificate is used with SSH. If a KeyUsage extension is present in a certificate for the four signature algorithms, the digitalSignature bit MUST be set. If it is present for the ecmqv-sha2 key exchange method, the keyAgreement bit MUST be set. Other certificates in the chain follow the usual RFC 5280 conventions.

The RFC also defines two ExtendedKeyUsage purpose identifiers, both optional: id-kp-secureShellClient ({ id-kp 21 }) for a key used by an SSH client and id-kp-secureShellServer ({ id-kp 22 }) for a key used by an SSH server. If the extension is present, the certificate MUST be used only for one of the listed purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: An ID card can say what it is good for, like 'for the front door only' or 'for the back door only', and the guard must obey that.

sections.title: Signature Encoding
sections.content:
Signing and verifying work the same way as with the matching non-certificate algorithms. Each signature starts with a string naming the underlying algorithm.

  • x509v3-ssh-dss: Digital Signature Standard with SHA-1; the blob holds r then s as fixed-length 160-bit integers. Same as ssh-dss in RFC 4253.
  • x509v3-ssh-rsa: RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 with SHA-1. Same as ssh-rsa in RFC 4253.
  • x509v3-rsa2048-sha256: RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 with SHA-256, and the RSA modulus MUST be at least 2048 bits. The signature string is rsa2048-sha256.
  • x509v3-ecdsa-sha2-*: ECDSA with the SHA2 family, with the hash chosen from the key size as in RFC 5656. The blob is two mpint values, r and s.

The x509v3-rsa2048-sha256 format is the only one with no earlier non-certificate SSH equivalent. It exists to offer an RSA format that fits current key size and hash recommendations; the RFC cites NIST draft guidance that treats RSA below 2048 bits or SHA-1 as deprecated from 2011 through 2013.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of ID card is signed with a particular pen. The new 'strong pen' option requires a thick, hard-to-forge signature.

sections.title: Where These Algorithms Are Used and Host Matching
sections.content:
The new algorithms SHOULD be accepted anywhere SSH uses public keys, including publickey and hostbased user authentication and several key exchange replies (SSH_MSG_KEXDH_REPLY, SSH_MSG_KEXRSA_PUBKEY, SSH_MSG_KEXGSS_HOSTKEY, SSH_MSG_KEX_ECDH_REPLY and SSH_MSG_KEX_ECMQV_REPLY). When such a key goes into a hash, the exact bytes sent on the wire must be hashed. Implementations MUST NOT drop chain certificates or OCSP responses or change their encoding, or the two peers will compute different hashes.

For user authentication, how certificates map to user names is left to implementers and administrators. For server authentication, the RFC RECOMMENDED mechanism uses the subjectAlternativeName extension with dNSName or iPAddress entries, and multiple entries are allowed. If the client's reference identifier is a DNS name, the server is checked using the rules of RFC 6125, and a DNS-ID may use a wildcard character as the complete left-most label. If it is an IP address, the client SHOULD convert it to network byte order octets and compare with an iPAddress entry. Local policy may disable this or add constraints.
sections.plainLanguage: When a server shows its ID card, you check that the name on the card matches the place you meant to visit. Everything on the card must be kept exactly as sent when double-checking.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Because the new algorithms are built on existing SSH ones, most SSH security considerations still apply. Implementers must also consider issues specific to certificates in a public key infrastructure, such as expired certificates and revocation lists. The reader is pointed to the security sections of RFC 5280, RFC 2560, RFC 4253 and RFC 4252.

Implementations SHOULD NOT use revoked certificates, since common causes of revocation (a compromised private key, or a certificate issued to the wrong party) mean the needed authentication properties no longer hold. An attempt to use a revoked certificate, or a missing response when the certificate says OCSP is used, SHOULD be logged with the date, time, certificate identity and apparent origin IP address.

IANA is asked to register the four algorithm names (the ECDSA one as a family of names beginning with x509v3-ecdsa-sha2- without an at-sign) in the Public Key Algorithm Names registry. The two object identifiers come from an arc delegated by IANA to the PKIX Working Group.
sections.plainLanguage: If an ID card was stolen or given to the wrong person, it gets cancelled and nobody should accept it. Writing down attempts to use a cancelled card helps catch trouble.

data.title: x509v3 public key data
data.code:
string  "x509v3-ssh-dss" / "x509v3-ssh-rsa" /
        "x509v3-rsa2048-sha256" / "x509v3-ecdsa-sha2-[identifier]"
uint32  certificate-count
string  certificate[1..certificate-count]
uint32  ocsp-response-count
string  ocsp-response[0..ocsp-response-count]
